extracted.intended_audience: biologists, naturalists, and scientifically literate readers interested in evolutionary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment and conceptualization of the causal factors that drive organic evolution (primordial physico-chemical actions, natural selection, sexual/fortuitous variation, and inheritance of functionally-produced modifications), with attention to embryological evidence and stages of increasing importance among factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primordial factor — direct action of the medium
rubrics_metrics.description: The direct physico-chemical action of the medium (environment) on organisms is the primordial factor of organic evolution: differential exposure of parts to incident forces causes initial changes from homogeneity to heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that the first evolutionary step must be the differentiation of external surface from internal contents because parts differently exposed to the environment will change first. The primordial factor initiates primary differentiations in protoplasm and continues to co-operate with natural selection throughout evolutionary history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface-origin of organs (blastoderm origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: All organs forming the adult originate from a superficial layer or blastoderm; organization begins on the surface because the surface receives environmental influences initiating instrumentalities for converse with the medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embryological development shows that the blastoderm gives rise to epidermis, nervous system, alimentary canal parts, etc.; this surface-origin explains why sense organs and nervous tissues originate from epidermal infoldings. The argument uses developmental morphology to infer causal relationships between environment and organogenesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation of germ layers (epiblast, hypoblast, mesoblast) and functional consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: From the external epiblast arise epidermis, nervous system, and sense organs; from the introverted hypoblast arise alimentary canal and related secretory linings; from the mesoblast originate internal structures (bones, muscles, heart, blood-vessels) that never directly converse with the environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This embryological partitioning is used as evidence that structures interacting with the environment arise from externally-originating layers while wholly internal structures derive from the mesoblast. The text notes minor qualifications but treats the broad functional distinctions as significant for interpreting evolutionary origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection as a co-operator and later predominant factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection acts on variations and becomes increasingly important as life becomes more differentiated and competitive; yet it can only 'take advantage of' structural changes initiated by the medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural selection is not presented as the sole originator of structure; it removes rudimentary or disadvantageous traits (e.g., deeper-seated nervous centres are favored against surface ones) and amplifies favourable variations. The text emphasizes that selection operates 'under subjection' to earlier environmental initiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance of functionally-produced modifications (use and disuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifications produced by function (use and disuse of parts) can be inherited and thus act as an important evolutionary factor, especially in higher organisms where functional changes become heritable and may be the chief factor in humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author stresses reviving attention to this factor (often associated with Lamarckian ideas), arguing it has been improperly ignored by some modern naturalists. If true, it bears on mental phenomena, moral intuitions, and sociological change. The text contrasts its action with natural selection across stages of complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortuitous (sexual) variation as a source of novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes associated with conjugation and sexual generation introduce frequent and marked fortuitous variations (constitutional mixtures) that may produce deviations in structure, some of which are suppressed and some preserved by natural selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As forms of life multiply and competition increases, fortuitous variations that affect struggle with enemies/competitors gain importance; in plants and relatively inactive animals natural selection on such variations is especially significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative shifting importance of factors over evolutionary time
rubrics_metrics.description: The various factors (primordial environmental action, natural selection, inheritance of functional modifications, fortuitous variation) change in relative importance at successive stages: primordial factor leads early, selection grows with differentiation and competition, and inheritance of functional changes may dominate in highest organisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text sketches (speculatively) that primordial action fixed starting points, natural selection became predominant with complexity, and inheritance of functionally produced modifications increased importance with activity and organization—possibly chief among civilized humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embryological evidence as test and guide for evolutionary hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Concurrent testimony from embryologists showing infoldings and tissue origins (e.g., nervous system and eyes from epidermis) provides evidence that challenges naive expectations from natural selection alone and supports environment-initiated origins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embryological facts (e.g., ganglion-cells derived from epithelial surface cells; eyes and sense organs arising from epidermal infoldings) are used to infer mechanisms and to question whether natural selection alone could account for such roundabout embryonic transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instability of the homogeneous to heterogeneous as a universal principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Both inorganic and primitive organic matter follow a universal tendency for homogeneous masses to pass into heterogeneous states; in early protoplasm this leads inevitably to superficial/internal differentiation under incident forces of the medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The argument generalizes physical-chemical principles to biological origins: without inherited cyclical metamorphoses there could be no spontaneous variation for selection; instead, environmental incident forces produce the first unlikenesses that seed further evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental evidence: light plus oxygen effects on protoplasm (mechanism for cell-wall formation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments show light in the presence of oxygen destroys minute protoplasmic portions by oxidation; on larger masses this would produce an altered envelope protecting unchanged protoplasm, i.e., a rudimentary cell-wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a concrete example where environmental physico-chemical action produces structural differentiation (supporting the primordial-factor thesis). The authors concluded that 'light and oxygen together accomplishing what neither can do alone'—a gradual oxidation leading to changed outer matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological caution: balance inductive and deductive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: While a priori reasoning is dangerous in biology, deductive considerations may be used to test whether their results coincide with inductive inferences; scientific inquiry must avoid adopting creeds and remain open to multiple causal explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly warns against adopting doctrinal certainty ('science commits suicide when it adopts a creed') and urges comparing deductive conceptions with inductive evidence. This is a methodological criterion for evaluating evolutionary claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociological and psychological implications guide importance of hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance or rejection of inheritance of functionally-produced modifications affects theories of mental phenomena, genesis of moral intuitions, and sociological beliefs about how institutions mould populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that because these hypotheses have wide downstream effects on views of life, mind, morals, and politics, resolving which is true demands close scientific attention. This elevates the practical stakes for adjudicating theoretical claims.
